argument_macro_structure.dominant_argument_form: Modal ontological argument with a priori necessity claim, defended via neoclassical theism
argument_macro_structure.premise_explicitness: explicit formalized premises and inference rules

argumentative_quality.premise_acceptability: moderate to high within modal theistic framework

distinctions_drawn: existence in understanding vs existence in reality
classical actus purus vs neoclassical modal coextensiveness
perfection as being vs perfection as becoming
unsurpassable by all beings vs unsurpassable by all beings save self in future states
existence as predicate vs existence as modal predicate
explicit_definitions_given: God = that than which none greater can be conceived
q = there is a perfect being
modal coextensiveness = God covers actual and possible territory with complete adequacy
actuality = decision among competitive alternative possibilities

dialectical_engagement.objection_handling: rebuts objections by revising the conception of God rather than abandoning the argument
objections_raised: Kant: existence is not a predicate
Classical actus purus entails contradictions (green/not-green, infinity, necessity of actuality)
Abstract perfection cannot bridge to concrete existence

method_and_evidence.evidence_type: formal logic, conceptual analysis, counterexamples, historical theological distinctions

philosophical_orientation.grounding: analytic philosophy of religion, modal logic, process/neoclassical theism
philosophical_orientation.sentiment: defends a revised ontological argument against classical objections
philosophical_orientation.thematic_focus: modal necessity, divine perfection, existence vs actuality, potentiality in God

structural_organization.structure_type: historical introduction, formal argument, thesis defense, objections and replies, conclusion

summary_of_core_decisions: The essay's structural core is a modal-logical reformulation of Anselm's ontological argument, grounded in Hartshorne's neoclassical distinction between abstract necessary existence and concrete contingent actuality, with the central thesis that possibility and being coincide in God.
